part.text: {"type":"finish","output":"The synthetic evidence set E01-E10 outlines a queue incident spanning 08:00-10:00. E10 excludes infrastructure noise (no deploy, schema change, host restart, network route change, or credential rotation), narrowing the target set. E01-E02 establish the trigger: queue depth grew from 120 to 1,850 while worker count was constant at 8. E03 confirms the operational impact: median latency rose from 1.8s to 14.2s. E04 is pivotal - the system's own compute resources were only 43% CPU, 51% memory, 22% disk, so the working pool was not saturated. E05 characterizes the upstream constraint: dependency B began rejecting 31% of outbound requests with HTTP 429. E06 shows the retry mechanism reacted with a 420% increase in retry volume under exponential backoff capped at three attempts. E07 is a near-experiment: scaling workers 8 to 16 moved queue depth only 6% in ten minutes, which is far short of halving the backlog that a throughput-doubling hypothesis would predict. E08 is a second controlled test: disabling retries for dependency B cut queue depth 38% in six minutes while raising the direct failure rate. E09 shows the deliberate intervention: raising rate limits reduced 429s below 1% and the queue settled under 150 in eleven minutes. The most likely primary cause is rate limiting imposed by dependency B, which surfaced at 09:15 as a recurring 429 response. The queue began growing at 09:00-09:10, and E10 rules out local changes, so the growth is consistent with a workload or upstream-driven event rather than an internal regression. E04 rules out internal resource exhaustion. E07 rules out worker-pool under-capacity. E08 and E09 form a cause-effect pair: removing the retry surge reduced the backlog, and raising the limit resolved it nearly completely. That chain is the strongest available evidence of causation because it moves the dependent variable twice in the expected directions while controlling for the same system. Secondary mechanisms are amplifiers. The 420% retry burst contributed meaningfully: each task received up to three attempts, and 31% of base traffic failing generated a cascade of re-entries that inflated the effective task count and, in turn, the queue. Retry volume creates a feedback loop: latency rises, timeouts rise, attempts rise, raw entries rise. E08's 38% decrease demonstrates the magnitude of that amplification. Adding workers (E07) had limited effect for three reasons. First, the bottleneck was not local compute: E04 notes 43% CPU and 51% memory, so extra workers were largely idle resources. Second, workers that hit dependency B still waited for rate-limit windows; doubling the pool doubles the concurrency hitting a 429-constrained end point, so latency per attempt (E03) is dominated by plan-limited wait time, not dispatch capacity. Third, the queue length after E07 remained high because the effective throughput of the 429-locked stages was constrained externally, so the incremental capacity translated into negligible progress, entirely consistent with the observed 6% change. The retry policy deserves assessment. Exponential backoff with a maximum of three retries is a reasonable defensive posture, but E06 shows the volume rise (420%) was disproportionate to the retry ceiling, meaning the policy lacked back-pressure, jitter coordination across workers, or circuit-breaker behavior. A fixed maximum of three is insufficient when the upstream limit persists: tasks exhausted all attempts quickly, then failed, then either were re-enqueued by the parent flow or were retried as new tasks at the application layer, so the effective retry count exceeded the declared cap. The policy also has no dependency-aware count. Under a 31% failure rate, unconditional retries double the inbound work. Assessment: moderate to low quality for this scenario. The uncertainty set is material. E05- E09 give no throughput trace, so we cannot separate request inflation from timeout inflation. We cannot identify which tenant or which flow generated the surge, since only aggregate samples are presented. The queue data points are ten-second snapshots, so peaks and valleys could be missed. E04 samples utilization at a single instant and do not distinguish burst patterns. Finally, E09 notes restriction removal resolved the incident, but we do not know whether the rate-limit change was already scheduled or was a one-off adjustment, which affects the lasting validity of the conclusion. A plausible alternative hypothesis is that a spike in inbound request volume drove the queue: consumers posted many tasks within a short window, the queue filled, and the retry layer merely mutated the symptom. That hypothesis is less supported for three reasons: E04 shows spare task capacity, which a genuine inbound flood would consume more aggressively; E07 shows capacity scaling produced no response, which a volume surge would have absorbed; and E08/E09 show the queue tracked the upstream limit and not the inbound pattern. The alternative is also unable to explain why the incident resolved specifically after rate-limit expansion, unless we assume the limit increase coincided with traffic normalization, an assumption contradicted by controlled observations. Consequently, the primary cause is the external rate limit, with the retry amplification the strongest amplifier and latency metric distortion as a secondary effect. Staged remediation: first, instrument rate-limit telemetry: log per-dependency, per-tenant 429 counts, buckets, and queue latency lanes. Second, add a circuit breaker: trip after, say, five consecutive 429 bursts per minute, then shed load or shed the specific dependency, and immediately disable retries on that dependency until it is half-open. Third, retro-adapt the retry policy: jitter plus a shorter maximum, one retry for 429, and a dependency-scoped capability. Fourth, right-size the work pool: hold workers constant, add scaling policy on CPU and queue-occupancy, never on raw queue depth while blocked. Fifth, quarantine the surge: tag failing requests with retry-ack or orphan checks so rejected attempts are not re-enqueued by the parent. Sixth, verify with a twenty-minute test: reproduce a synthetic limit reduction and confirm queue-depth and retry-load drop in lockstep. The analysis is limited by snapshot sampling, so real dashboards with continuous metrics, per-dependency 429 breakdowns, and retry counters would materially upgrade confidence.","data":{"executive_summary":"Between 09:00 and 10:00, queue depth rose from 120 to 1,850 while local compute stayed healthy at 43% CPU, 51% memory, and 22% disk. Dependency B began returning HTTP 429 on 31% of outbound calls, and retry volume jumped 420% with exponential backoff capped at three attempts. Scaling workers from 8 to 16 cut queue depth only 6%, excluding worker capacity as the cause. Disabling retries temporarily dropped queue depth 38% in six minutes, and after rate limits were raised, 429s fell below 1% and the queue settled under 150. No deploy, schema change, restart, or credential rotation occurred.
